title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in the Elderly: A Case Identified With Genetic Screening
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, breast cancer, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (status post pulmonary vein and cavo-tricuspid isolation), and recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding on rivaroxaban was admitted for left atrial appendage closure.

Postoperatively, she received one dose of lisinopril, which led to profound hypotension requiring intravenous fluids and a low-dose vasopressor. She had a transient troponin elevation thought to be due to demand ischemia.

Further history revealed that one of her sons died suddenly in his early 50s (reported as a “heart attack”). The patient also endorsed many years of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, lower extremity edema, chest tightness, and orthopnea, with recurrent episodes of orthostatic hypotension.

A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated:
  • Left ventricular ejection fraction 67%  
  • LV internal diastolic diameter 4.4 cm (normal 3.5–6.5 cm)  
  • Right ventricular systolic pressure 40 mm Hg (normal <36 mm Hg)  
  • LV outflow tract gradient <30 mm Hg  
  • Global longitudinal strain −15% with reduced antero-septal strain

Left and right heart catheterization showed no obstructive coronary artery disease. Hemodynamic measurements were:
  • Pulmonary arterial wedge pressure 36 mm Hg  
  • Mean pulmonary arterial pressure 45 mm Hg  
  • Right ventricular systolic pressure 62 mm Hg  
  • Right atrial pressure 12 mm Hg
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Obstructive coronary artery disease was excluded by invasive angiography — “no obstructive coronary artery disease was found.”  
2. Systemic and secondary causes of LVH (eg, mitochondrial myopathies, storage diseases, amyloid, sarcoid, hemochromatosis, athletic heart, hypertensive cardiomyopathy, valvular lesions) were initially considered as alternatives — “There are many systemic disorders (mitochondrial myopathies, storage diseases, amyloid, sarcoid, hemochromatosis) or secondary causes of LVH (athletic heart, hypertensive cardiomyopathy, and valvular lesions) different from inherited HCM that can all cause a thickening of the LV wall.” and ultimately deprioritized in the absence of supporting findings — “In the lack of other etiologies that could explain LVH in adults, diagnosis could possibly be HCM.”  
3. Hereditary amyloid cardiomyopathy was on the differential because of infiltrative potential — “Differentials included hereditary amyloid cardiomyopathy, and less likely HCM.”  
4. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was suspected given the family history, atypical strain pattern, and exclusion of other causes — “With the suspicious family history (son’s sudden and premature death without a clear etiology), regular episodes of orthostatic hypotension, and heart failure symptoms, genetic screening for cardiomyopathies was performed.”  
5. HCM was confirmed by genetic testing and CMR findings of asymmetric hypertrophy and fibrosis — “she was heterozygous for an abnormal MYBPC3 gene with a pathogenic mutation p.E1085 commonly associated with HCM,” and CMR “demonstrated asymmetric thickening of the LV wall with an antero-septal wall thickness up to 17 mm, abnormal delayed enhancement … suggestive of asymmetric HCM.”
